questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Radii of Gyration Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082741/assets/5b8ddb36e814517af21d790374e1fb192141bd6ef0fd99e83a147c6ed5a62aea.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=3x,$ $x=1,$ $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{45}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3x}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3x}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{M}{45}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{45}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3x}{x}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{45}{\int }_{1}^{2}{[{x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{45}{\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{5}+9{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{45}{\int }_{1}^{2}12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{45}[2{x}^{6}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{45}\cdot (128-2) \\  & =\frac{14M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{14M}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{14}{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ the line $y=1,$ and the $y$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{28M}{3}x{y}^{3}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le 1}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{28M}{3}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{28M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{1}x{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{28M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{6}x{y}^{6}]}_{y={x}^{3}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{14M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-{x}^{19}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{14M}{9}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{20}{x}^{20}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{14M}{9}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{20}) \\  & =\frac{14M}{9}\cdot \frac{9}{20} \\  & =\frac{7M}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{7M}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 6.$ Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{9\pi }{y}^{2}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{6},\,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{9\pi }{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{9\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}{r}^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{9\pi }({\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{9\pi }\cdot 36\cdot {[\frac{\theta }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{9\pi }\cdot 36\cdot \pi  \\  & =4M.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{4M\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{2}{9\pi }M({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{2}{9\pi }M{r}^{2}.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{5}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M({\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M\cdot \frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }M\cdot \frac{9}{2}\cdot {[\frac{\theta }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }\cdot \pi  \\  & =M.\end{aligned}
$$
